newsitem.title: BRAZIL: Couple in Brazil's vote scandal get death threats.
newsitem.headline: Couple in Brazil's vote scandal get death threats.

text.p: A politician who purportedly brought to light a money-for-votes scandal that has rocked the Brazilian government on Monday denied involvement and said she and her husband had received anonymous death threats.

Deputy Celia Mendes said she had no knowledge of tapes made by a mysterious "Mr X" on which lawmakers allegedly confessed to receiving $190,000 in bribes for voting in favour of President Fernando Henrique Cardoso's re-election bid.
She said her husband, Narciso, was also not involved, but that as a result of media reports claiming they had made the tapes, she had had to request police protection.

"I am not Mrs Y and my husband is not Mr X," Mendes told reporters. "This deputy never recorded any conversations with government authorities. Likewise, it's unknown to me that my husband, the businessman Narciso Mendes, did such a thing."

Financial markets took a beating last week after the Folha de Sao Paulo newspaper published a story saying five deputies from the state of Acre had been bribed to vote in favour of a bill allowing presidents, governors and mayors to stand again.
Regarded as one of Cardoso's greatest political triumphs, the re-election bill was passed by the lower house in January and was making its way through the Senate.
Cardoso has denied any wrong-doing and his communications minister, Sergio Motta, a close friend and principal political aide, angrily dismissed reports that he was involved.
In a statement, Mendes said she and her husband had received numerous death threats since the scandal broke.
"Due to these reports, which were never confirmed, my family has been the victim of anonymous telephone calls which tell us our lives are in danger," she said.
Mendes' husband, himself a former federal legislator, was identified by the politicians implicated in the scam and by newspapers as the "Mr X" who taped the conversations.
The scandal has hit the government at a difficult time as it is pushing for key reforms to the civil service and the pensions system to shore up public sector finances.
A Congress probe into the scam was due to report on Tuesday.

Opposition parties were pushing for a wide-ranging parliamentary inquiry, which would likely stall all work in Congress as happened during impeachment proceedings against former president Fernando Collor.
